title: Stop Doing L-sit to V-sit Wrong: Train Your hip leverage Instead
description: Sit on the floor, press down, and lift your legs toward your chest. Your V-sit angle is the test: how high your straight legs climb while your hips stay tall. Most skinny guys train it in a way that stalls the angle for months. Here is the hip leverage fix.

scenes.narration: Sit on the floor with your legs straight out in front of you and your hands flat beside your hips. Press down hard, lift your body just off the floor, and raise your straight legs as high as they will go while your chest stays tall. Hold the highest clean position for three seconds and look at the angle: are your legs below horizontal, at horizontal, or climbing above it toward your chest? That angle, held honestly with straight knees and no leaning back, is your number. Keep it. Most guys train this movement in a way that guarantees the angle never changes, and by the end I will show you the lever you have been ignoring.

scenes.label: LEGS ABOVE HORIZONTAL IS THE LINE
scenes.sub: below horizontal: building - 90 deg: true V-sit
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Legs held forty-five degrees above horizontal for three clean seconds, knees locked and chest tall, is certified hip leverage. Below horizontal, you are in the building zone, where most of the work is still being done by momentum and hope. A true V-sit, legs near vertical with your body folded into a sharp V, is the far end of this road and takes most people a year or more. Grade yourself honestly, because this test has a famous cheat: leaning back. Every centimeter your chest falls backward buys leg height you did not earn, paid for by geometry instead of hip flexors. The angle only counts at the posture you could hold in a photograph. Film one attempt from the side and the truth takes three seconds to see. Your number is the angle in the photograph, not the angle in your memory.

Look at the hip. Raising a straight leg is a lever problem: your leg is a long beam, your hip joint is the hinge, and your hip flexors must produce enough torque to lift the beam against gravity. Torque is force times distance, and a straight leg puts almost all of its weight at the far end of the beam, which is why the last thirty degrees feel impossible while the first thirty feel free. Two muscles split this bill. The psoas, deep in your trunk, starts the lift. The rectus femoris, crossing both hip and knee, finishes it, and it can only pull hard when the knee stays straight. Bend the knee and the beam shortens, the price drops, and the training effect evaporates. The V-sit is not a stomach exercise with leg decoration. It is a hip lever, priced by leg length, paid by flexors most people have never trained at this angle.

beats.title: TORQUE = FORCE x DISTANCE
lines: A straight leg is a long beam.

scenes.narration: The second half of this skill is compression, the ability to fold at the hips while the spine stays long. Watch a gymnast fold and a beginner fold and you are watching two different joints. The gymnast folds at the hips, chest reaching toward the shins, pelvis rotating forward. The beginner folds at the lower back, rounding into a C shape, which moves the chest away from the legs even as the legs rise. Compression strength is its own trainable quality: the deep trunk muscles that posteriorly and anteriorly tilt the pelvis on command. This is why your angle can stall even as your hip flexors get stronger. The beam is rising, but the wall it must approach keeps retreating. Train the fold and the lift together and the angle closes from both sides. Train only the lift and you are raising a beam toward a wall that walks away.

beats.text: FOLD AT THE HIPS, NOT THE BACK
THE ANGLE CLOSES FROM BOTH SIDES

scenes.narration: The drill that builds both halves is the seated leg lift. Sit tall with your hands on the floor beside your thighs, and lift one straight leg as high as it goes without leaning back, ten slow reps per side. It looks like a mobility exercise and behaves like strength training, because at the top of the lift your hip flexor is working at its shortest length, the exact range the V-sit grades. Three sets, three times a week. When one leg floats to forty-five degrees without your chest moving, the pair will follow within weeks.

beats.text: THE SHORT RANGE IS THE TEST

scenes.narration: Your advantage is hiding in the lever equation. The price of the lift is the weight of your legs at the end of a long beam, and skinny legs are lighter beams. The hip flexors of a light guy reach the high angles sooner, practice more quality reps per session, and recover faster between them. There is a second, sneakier advantage: compression favors the compact. A shorter trunk folds closer to the thighs with less soft tissue in the way, which is why gymnastics, the sport that owns this skill, selects for exactly your build. The big guy grinding V-sits is fighting his own mass at the hinge and his own bulk at the fold. You are fighting neither. Your only opponent is a pair of untrained hip flexors, and untrained is the most fixable diagnosis in this entire season.
Press down and lift with me. Legs straight, toes pointed, chest tall, fifteen seconds. If the legs sink below horizontal, bend one knee and keep going. Go.

Here is the fix, the way to train this so the angle actually moves. Stop swinging. Every kicked rep teaches your nervous system that momentum is the strategy, and momentum does not show up on test day. Lift slowly, two seconds up, two seconds down, and stop the set when the chest starts to lean. Stop testing daily. The angle is a monthly measurement, not a daily mood; test it once a month, train the pieces three times a week. Stop skipping the support hold: your hands must press you tall before the legs can climb, so open every session with three twenty-second support holds. And stop stretching your hamstrings as your main plan. Tight hamstrings limit some people, but for most skinny guys the ceiling is flexor strength at short length, not length at the back of the leg. The weekly shape is simple: seated leg lifts, support holds, and one honest angle check at the end of the month. Leverage improves when the hinge is trained at the angle the test grades. Train the hinge there.

So, your angle. Below horizontal with a tall chest: the hinge is honest and untrained, the best starting position there is. At horizontal for three clean seconds: the L-sit is yours and the V is under construction. Above forty-five degrees: your hip leverage is certified, and compression work is now your main road. Retest in thirty days, filmed from the side, chest tall, three-second hold at the top. Put your angle in the comments. Just the number, in degrees as best you can judge it. The photograph does not flatter and does not lie, and the angle in it is the only progress report this skill issues. Train the hinge, fold the wall toward the beam, and the number moves.
A long beam, a strong hinge, and a fold that closes the gap. That is the V-sit. Subscribe, and bring me your new angle in thirty days. This is {channel}. Train the cable.
